title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
key_facts: Researchers, mainly from David Baker's lab at the University of Washington, used AI design tools to make new protein-cutting enzymes (proteases).
They kept the catalytic core of two protease types, zinc and cysteine, and redesigned the rest using RFdiffusion2 and ProteinMPNN.
For the cysteine protease, 13 designs worked, a 19 percent success rate, all less active than the yeast original.
For the zinc protease, 35 of 38 designs with a placed water molecule showed some activity versus 14 of 89 without.
Random-mutation tweaks made some versions much more active; a v2 zinc version was 30 times more active than the original design.
They built zinc proteases that cut proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia in cells.
Delivery to cells and immune reactions are major hurdles for any therapy.
quote_evidence: The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half
there are considerable hurdles that would need to be cleared before we could potentially start developing therapies using this technology.
why_it_matters_hint: Shows AI can design working enzymes from scratch, though activity is still below natural ones.
notes: The article states some rate-increase figures with lost superscripts (e.g. '109'); those figures are not used.
